sentences.text: Jobaria was a primitive sauropod measuring approximately 18.2 meters in length and weighing about 22.4 tonnes.
This dinosaur possessed a short neck containing only 12 vertebrae and large teeth adapted for its diet.
Its skull was constructed from fragile bones featuring a robust dome and large openings for the nose.
The head was small, high, and rounded with a short snout and spoon-shaped teeth similar to those of Camarasaurus.
Dorsal vertebrae were very simple structures that lacked air sacs and possessed simple spines.
Limb proportions were primitive, with forelimbs not as elongated relative to the hindlimbs as seen in Brachiosaurus.
Over 95 percent of the skeleton is preserved, making it one of the most complete sauropods ever discovered.
Some estimates suggest the animal reached lengths of 21 meters, a height of 4.5 meters, and a weight of 18 tonnes.
Jobaria is the only known valid sauropod discovered in the Tiouraren formation.
The species name tiguidensis refers to the specific cliff of Tiguidi where the fossils were unearthed.
Remains were found in the Ingal bei Agadez region of Niger by an expedition led by Paul Sereno in 1999.
Multiple specimens, including an articulated adult and partial adults and juveniles, provide information on 95 percent of the animal, including clavicles and gastralia.
The name Jobaria comes from Jobar, a mythical animal of the Tuareg people who inhabit the Sahara desert region.
Paul Sereno suggested Jobaria could rear up on its hind legs based on comparisons of limb bone ratios with extant elephants.
The classification of Jobaria is uncertain, with interpretations ranging from a basal macronarian to a non-neosauropod eusauropod.
Re-interpretation of sediments suggests Jobaria lived between 167 and 161 million years ago during the Bathonian to Oxfordian stages of the Middle Jurassic.
Originally, sediments were thought to date to the Early Cretaceous, suggesting Jobaria lived approximately 132 million years ago.
Reinterpretation of sediments indicates Jobaria likely lived between 167 and 161 million years ago during the Bathonian to Oxfordian stages of the Middle Jurassic.
The Paleobiology Database lists the time range for Jobaria as Oxfordian to Tithonian, spanning from 161.5 to 143.1 million years ago.
